column2: ✅✅ LEAD 6 REFUTED ON ITS OWN ASSUMPTIONS — a permanent buydown does NOT create negative equity; it makes the buyer MORE protected against a price decline than an identical market-rate buyer
column3: HOMER arithmetic, $300K loan, 30yr, DHI's own issuer-stated rates (backlog 4.9% vs market ~6.5%, a 1.6ppt buydown), assuming the FULL buydown cost is embedded in the price (the thesis's own worst case, costed at AEI's ppt->cost conversion = ~6.2% of loan = ~$18,462): BREAK-EVEN HOLD = 4.0 YEARS. At 5 years the buydown buyer is AHEAD by ~$5,520. At every price-decline level tested (0/-3/-5/-10%) the buydown buyer holds MORE equity than the market-rate buyer; at -10% the MARKET-RATE buyer goes underwater first (-$1,040) while the buydown buyer is still positive (+$4,700).
column4: Transcript claim: buyers 'may potentially be upside down when they try to sell'
column6: HOMER computation on DHI issuer-stated rates + AEI cost conversion; tenure benchmark NAR (SECONDARY, via search summary)
column8: ★★★ WHY THE CLAIM FAILS: it counts the embedded price premium and IGNORES the two things a lower rate does. (1) FASTER AMORTIZATION -- at 4.9% vs 6.5%, ~$5,740 MORE principal is retired over five years. (2) CUMULATIVE PAYMENT SAVINGS -- ~$18,241 over five years. Total benefit ~$23,981 against a ~$18,462 premium. => THE BUYDOWN DOES NOT CREATE NEGATIVE EQUITY. It creates a ~6% price premium that a PRICE DECLINE would then expose -- and those are DIFFERENT CLAIMS WITH DIFFERENT INSTRUMENTS. The transcript's own text concedes the conditionality ('only works in your favor if home values keep climbing') and then presents the buydown itself as the cause. ★★ AND THE RELATIVE RESULT IS THE STRONGER ONE: a price decline hits BOTH buyers equally, so it cannot change their RELATIVE position -- and the buydown buyer, having amortized faster, is BETTER protected. The market-rate buyer goes underwater FIRST. ★★★ THE REAL DISCRIMINATOR IS HOLD PERIOD, NOT THE BUYDOWN: under ~4 years the buydown buyer is behind; over it they are ahead. => TESTED AGAINST THE POPULATION: NAR median ACTUAL tenure before selling is ~11 YEARS (a record high) and median EXPECTED tenure ~15 years, with 28% calling it a forever home. THE TYPICAL BUYER CLEARS THE 4.0-YEAR BREAK-EVEN BY ROUGHLY SEVEN YEARS. ★ AND THE BUYDOWN IS SELF-PROTECTING ON THAT DIMENSION: a borrower at 4.9% facing a 6.5% market is RATE-LOCKED-IN, which EXTENDS hold and pushes them further past break-even. The mechanism is pointed at a behaviour moving AWAY from it. ⚠️⚠️ WHERE THE RESIDUAL RISK GENUINELY LIVES, AND I DO NOT HOLD IT: the LEFT TAIL. Median tenure says nothing about the share who move inside four years, and FIRST-TIME buyers -- 64% of DHI Mortgage's book -- are the cohort most exposed to early moves (job change, family formation). THE DISTRIBUTION, NOT THE MEDIAN, IS THE MISSING INSTRUMENT. ⚠️ ASSUMPTIONS STATED: full cost embedded (worst case; partial embedding leaves the buyer better off still); AEI's June-2025 ppt->cost conversion spliced onto DHI's July-2026 1.6ppt (DIRECTIONAL, not a measurement); 30yr term, no refi; SELLING COSTS (~6-8%) OMITTED and FHA MIP omitted -- both hit the two buyers EQUALLY so the RELATIVE conclusion is robust, but the ABSOLUTE equity figures are optimistic. => NO INSTRUMENT BUILT AND NONE NEEDED: the mechanism does not survive its own arithmetic. Lead 6 CLOSED as refuted, with the left-tail distribution named as the only thing that would revive it.
